questions.prompt: Why does `[x]() { ++x; }` fail to compile when `x` is a local `int`, and how does `mutable` fix it?
options: `x` is captured by `const int&` unless `mutable` switches it to `int&`.
Capturing `x` by value always makes `x` `const` everywhere in the enclosing function.
Lambdas cannot store non-static integer members without `mutable`.
The synthesized `operator()` is `const`-qualified by default, so `mutable` removes `const` to allow modifying the closure's copy of `x`.
questions.explanation: A lambda lowers to a closure class whose `operator()` is `const` by default (`[expr.prim.lambda.closure]/5`), preventing modification of by-value captured data members. Adding `mutable` drops the `const` qualifier from `operator()`, letting the closure mutate its own copy of `x` without changing the caller's `x`.

questions.prompt: Why does `auto bump = [&x]() { ++x; };` compile without `mutable`, even though `operator()` is still `const`?
options: The closure stores a reference member `int&`, and a `const` member function can mutate the object a reference member refers to.
Reference captures automatically add `mutable` to the lambda.
Inside a lambda, `operator()` becomes non-`const` whenever `&` appears in the capture list.
`++x` resolves to a global variable lookup instead of a closure member.
questions.explanation: In C++, `const` on a member function applies to the closure object's direct members, not deeply through pointers or references. Because `[&x]` gives the closure an `int&` member, `const` prevents rebinding that reference (impossible anyway), while `++x` mutates the external `int` freely.

questions.prompt: Inside a member function of `Widget`, what happens if you return `[=]() { return id; }` and the `Widget` is destroyed before the returned lambda runs?
options: It returns `42` safely because `[=]` copies `id` by value into the closure.
It copies `*this` by value in C++17 and later.
It stores the `this` pointer by value, so invoking the returned lambda after `Widget` dies reads through a dangling pointer (UB).
It fails to compile in C++17 and C++23.
questions.explanation: Inside a member function, `id` is `this->id`, so `[=]` implicitly captures the `this` pointer—not a copy of `id` or `*this`. Calling the closure after `Widget` is destroyed is undefined behavior. C++20 deprecated implicit `this` capture via `[=]` in favor of explicit `[=, this]` or by-value `[=, *this]`.

questions.prompt: What does the `static_assert` evaluate to when comparing two identical empty lambda expressions?
options: `true`, because captureless lambdas have a canonical empty closure type.
`false`, because each lambda expression generates its own unique unnamed closure type.
`true` in C++20+, since captureless lambdas became default-constructible.
Ill-formed, because lambdas cannot appear inside `decltype`.
questions.explanation: Under `[expr.prim.lambda.closure]/1`, every lambda expression introduces a unique unnamed class type distinct from all others—even with identical bodies and captures. Since C++20, lambdas are also valid in unevaluated operands like `decltype([]{})`.

questions.prompt: When `N` is a local `constexpr int N = 10;` variable inside `main`, why does `auto f = []() { return N + 1; };` compile with an empty capture list `[]`?
options: Reading `N` for its integral constant value does not odr-use `N`, so `[expr.prim.lambda.capture]` requires no capture.
All `constexpr` local variables are silently given static storage duration.
`[]` automatically captures local variables that fit in a CPU register.
It only compiles in C++23; C++20 required `[N]` here.
questions.explanation: A lambda may refer to a reaching local variable without capturing it if that variable is not odr-used (`[expr.prim.lambda.capture]/4`, `[basic.def.odr]`). Because `N + 1` reads `N`'s constant value immediately without taking `&N` or binding a reference to `N`, no capture is needed.

questions.prompt: Which restriction applies to C++23 lambdas declared with a `static` function call operator (`[](int x) static { ... }`)?
questions.code: auto scale = [](int x) static { return x * 2; };
options: They cannot convert to a plain function pointer.
They cannot be `constexpr`.
They cannot have any captures and cannot be combined with `mutable` or an explicit object parameter.
They can only appear at namespace scope.
questions.explanation: In C++23 (`[expr.prim.lambda.general]` and `[expr.prim.lambda.closure]`), making `operator()` a `static` member function removes the implicit closure object parameter (`this`), so the closure cannot access captured members (`capture-default` or captures are ill-formed), nor can `static` be combined with `mutable` or `this auto`.
